title: Structs
intro: Structs group named fields into one type of your own.

coming_from.go: A Rust struct is a Go struct with `name: Type` order. You must set every field when you build one (there are no zero values), and fields are private to their module until you mark them `pub`, not when they start with a lowercase letter. There is no struct embedding: a struct that holds another one keeps it in a named field.
coming_from.kotlin: A struct is a data class where you don't write the constructor: you build it with `User { name: ..., age: ... }`. Printing, `==` and copying are opt-in through `#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Clone)]` rather than given for free.
coming_from.python: A struct is your `@dataclass`, and `#[derive(Debug)]` is the generated `__repr__`. The set of fields is fixed, so you can't add a new attribute to a value later.
coming_from.typescript: A struct is like an `interface` plus an object literal, but every field must be given and the type is nominal. Another struct with the same fields is still not a `User`, and an optional field is written `Option<T>` ([Option](/learn/option/)), not `age?:`.
coming_from.java: A Rust `struct` is closest to a `record`: named fields, and every field must be given when you create one. Unlike a record, a field can be changed if the variable is `mut`. There's no constructor, no default values and no auto `toString` or `equals`; `#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]` adds them.
coming_from.csharp: A `struct` with `#[derive(Debug)]` is a lot like a positional `record`, but you build it with field names, like an object initializer where every property is `required`. There is no constructor and no default value for a missing field. It is not a C# `struct` in the value-type sense: `let b = a;` moves the value, it does not copy it.
coming_from.c: Rust structs look like C structs built with designated initializers, `.name = ...` becoming `name: ...`. Leaving a field out is a compile error instead of zero, and `#[derive(Debug)]` writes the print function for you. Rust may also reorder the fields in memory; `#[repr(C)]` asks for C's layout.
coming_from.cpp: A Rust `struct` is an aggregate built with designated initializers, but every field is required, so nothing is silently zeroed. `#[derive(Debug)]` stands in for the `operator<<` you would write by hand. Rust may reorder the fields in memory; `#[repr(C)]` asks for the order you wrote.

notes: `#[derive(Debug)]` asks the compiler to write the printing code for you, so `{u:?}` can print the whole struct. You can also derive `Clone`, `PartialEq` (for `==`), `Default`, and more.
`String::from("ana")` makes an owned `String` from text in your code. The Strings lesson, later, explains the two string types.
`User { age: 31, ..old }` builds a new value and takes every field you did not list from `old`. If it takes a `String` or other owned field, `old` loses it.
Fields are private outside their module unless marked `pub`. There is no capital-letter rule.

gotcha.title: Leaving fields out
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, fields you leave out become zero values: `Age` is 0 and `Active` is false. The code runs, and plenty of Go types are designed so that the zero value is useful.
gotcha.rust_sees: Rust has no automatic zero values. Every field must be given.
gotcha.why: Nothing here is unsafe; it is a different default. Is `age: 0` a real age, or a field you forgot? Is `port: 0` intended? Rust makes you say. When zeros really are what you want, ask for them explicitly with `Default`. (Go would use a `*int` for "unset"; Rust uses `Option<u32>`, [Option](/learn/option/).)

go.says: Go runs this and prints ana 0 false. Missing fields get their zero values, which Go treats as a feature, and many Go types are written so that the zero value works. Rust asks you to say it.

kotlin.says: Kotlin refuses this too: leaving out `age` and `active` is a compile error unless the class gives them defaults, like `val age: Int = 0`. The closest Rust tool is `#[derive(Default)]`, which defaults the whole struct, shown in the fix.

python.says: A dataclass won't let you skip fields either. Python raises a TypeError when you build the object, naming the two missing fields.
python.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class User:
    name: str
    age: int
    active: bool


u = User(name="ana")
print(u.name)

typescript.says: TypeScript refuses this too: an object typed as `User` must have every field, so `age` and `active` are reported as missing.
typescript.error: main.ts(7,7): error TS2739: Type '{ name: string; }' is missing the following properties from type 'User': age, active

java.says: A plain class fills missing fields with 0 and false, so this prints `ana 0 false` like Go. A record would refuse, because its constructor needs every field.

csharp.says: The object initializer fills only Name, and the rest get defaults, so it prints ana 0 False. Mark the properties `required` if you want the compiler to insist.

c.says: C sets the fields you leave out to zero, so this prints ana 0 0. Rust makes you give every field.

cpp.says: This compiles with a `-Wextra` warning about the missing fields, then prints `ana 0 false`. With brace initialization the left-out fields are zero, much like Go.

alias.py.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace


@dataclass
class Team:
    name: str
    members: list


a = Team("red", ["ana"])
b = a  # two names for one object
b.name = "blue"
print("a.name after b = a, b.name = 'blue':", a.name)

c = replace(a, name="green")  # a new object, but a shallow copy
c.members.append("bob")
print("a.members:", a.members)
print("same list object:", a.members is c.members)

copy-shallow.kt.code:
data class Team(val name: String, val members: MutableList<String>)

fun main() {
    val a = Team("red", mutableListOf("ana"))
    val b = a.copy(name = "blue")
    b.members.add("bob")
    println("a: $a")
    println("b: $b")
    println("same list object: ${a.members === b.members}")
}
